rows.en: This neon yellow ball ruling courts worldwide is actually a newcomer, just past fifty.
Tennis history spans well over a century, and for most of it the stars were white and black balls.
Black balls on bright grass, white balls on dark courts. The color changed with the background.
But when tennis stepped into the living-room TV, a strange problem appeared.
On black-and-white screens, a white ball crossing a white line simply vanished.
Cameras chased it, viewers squinted, but the star of the show was invisible.
Researchers hunted for the color that survived best on screen. The answer: fluorescent yellow.
On court and on screen, it stayed sharp against any background.
But one more problem: the rulebook recognized white balls only.
A better ball was found, yet the rules blocked its way in.
So why didn't the rules open the door right away?
The ITF spent two full years rolling yellow balls in real matches.
And in 1972, the yellow ball finally entered the rulebook.
The rules didn't erase white, they added yellow. White balls are still legal today.
Cut them open and they are identical inside. Only the coat changed color.
Even Wimbledon, loyal to white, finally gave in, in 1986, after 108 years.
In the end it wasn't players who made yellow the standard. It was the viewers' eyes.
That yellow ball bouncing across your screen tonight was a color approved for the viewer.
